source_text: Caro facta est anima, ut anima ostenderetur. Numquid ergo et caro anima facta est, ut caro manifestaretur? Si caro anima est, jam non anima est, sed caro. Si anima caro est, jam non caro est, sed anima. Ubi ergo caro, et ubi anima est, alterutrum facta est. Imo si neutrum sunt, dum alterutrum alterum fiunt, certe perversissimum, ut carnem nominantes, animam intelligamus, et animam significantes, carnem interpretemur. Omnia periclitabuntur aliter accipi quam sunt, et amittere quod sunt, dum aliter accipiuntur, si aliter quam sunt, cognominantur. Fides nominum, salus est proprietatum. Etiam cum demutantur qualitates, accipiunt vocabulorum possessiones. Verbi gratia, argilla excocta testae vocabulum suscipit; nec communicat cum vocabulo pristini generis, quia nec cum ipso genere. Proinde et anima Christi, caro facta, non potest non id esse quod facta est, et id non esse quod fuerit, aliud scilicet facta. Et quoniam proximum adhibuimus exemplum, plenius eo utemur. Certe enim testa ex argilla unum est corpus, unumque vocabulum, unius scilicet corporis. Nec potest dici et argilla; quia quod fuit, non est; quod autem non est, omnino non adhaeret. Ergo et anima caro facta, uniformis, solidata: scilicet singularitas tota est, et indiscreta substantia. In Christo vero invenimus animam et carnem simplicibus et nudis vocabulis editas, id est animam animam, et carnem carnem; nusquam animam carnem, aut carnem animam: quando ita nominari debuissent, si ita fuissent: sed etiam sibi quamque substantiam divise pronuntiatas ab ipso, utique pro duarum qualitatum distinctione, seorsum animam, et seorsum carnem. Quid anxia est, inquit, anima mea usque ad mortem? et: Panis quem ego dedero pro salute mundi, caro mea est. Porro, si anima caro fuisset, unum esset in Christo carnea anima, aut caro animalis. At cum dividit species, carnem et animam, duo ostendit: si duo, jam non unum; si non unum, jam nec anima carnalis, nec caro animalis; unum enim est anima caro, aut caro anima. Nisi et seorsum aliam gestabat animam, praeter eam quae caro erat, et aliam circumferebat carnem, praeter illam quae anima erat. Quod si una caro, et una anima; illa tristis usque ad mortem, et illa panis pro mundi salute; salvus est numerus duarum substantiarum, in suo genere distantium, excludens carneae animae unicam speciem.
thought_title: The Flesh and Soul of Christ
pass_a_gloss: The flesh was made soul, so that the soul might be shown. Therefore, was the flesh also made soul, so that the flesh might be manifested? If the flesh is soul, it is no longer soul, but flesh. If the soul is flesh, it is no longer flesh, but soul. Where, therefore, the flesh is, and where the soul is, one of the two has been made. Indeed, if neither of them is, while one is being made into the other, certainly it is most perverse, so that, naming flesh, we understand soul, and signifying soul, we interpret flesh. All things will be endangered to be taken otherwise than they are, and to lose what they are, while they are taken otherwise, if they are named otherwise than they are. The faith of names is the salvation of properties. Even when qualities are changed, they take on the possessions of words. For example, clay, when baked, takes on the name of earthenware; nor does it share with the name of its former kind, because it does not share with that kind itself. Therefore, the soul of Christ, made flesh, cannot but be what it has been made, and not be what it was, namely, something else made. And since we have used the nearest example, we will use it more fully. Certainly, the earthenware from the clay is one body, and one word, namely, of one body. Nor can it be said to be clay; because what it was, is not; what, however, is not, does not at all adhere. Therefore, the soul made flesh, is uniform, solidified: namely, the entirety is singularity, and undivided substance. In Christ, however, we find the soul and flesh expressed with simple and bare words, that is, soul as soul, and flesh as flesh; nowhere soul as flesh, or flesh as soul: when, indeed, they ought to have been so named, if they were so: but also each substance is pronounced separately by Him, undoubtedly for the distinction of two qualities, separately soul, and separately flesh. What is my soul troubled about, he says, until death? and: The bread which I will give for the salvation of the world, is my flesh. Further, if the soul had been flesh, there would be one fleshy soul, or animal flesh, in Christ. But since He divides the species, flesh and soul, He shows two: if two, then not one; if not one, then neither soul-flesh, nor flesh-soul; for one is soul-flesh, or flesh-soul. Unless He also carried another soul separately, besides that which was flesh, and carried another flesh separately, besides that which was soul. But if there is one flesh, and one soul; that one sorrowful until death, and that one bread for the salvation of the world; the number of the two substances, distinct in their kind, is saved, excluding the single species of flesh-soul.

pass_b_english: The flesh was made soul so that the soul might be shown. Was the flesh, then, also made soul so that the flesh might be manifested? If flesh is soul, it is no longer soul but flesh. If soul is flesh, it is no longer flesh but soul. Wherever flesh is and wherever soul is, one of the two has been turned into the other. Indeed, if neither exists while each becomes the other, it is utterly perverse: naming flesh, we would understand soul; signifying soul, we would interpret flesh. Everything risks being taken for what it is not and losing what it is, because it is being taken otherwise, if it is named otherwise than it is. The fidelity of names is the salvation of properties. Even when qualities change, they take possession of their words. For instance, clay, once baked, takes the name of earthenware; it no longer shares the name of its former kind, because it no longer shares that kind itself. Therefore the soul of Christ, made flesh, cannot fail to be what it has been made, and not be what it was — namely, something else now made. And since we have used the closest example, we will press it further. The earthenware from clay is certainly one body and one word — namely, of that one body. Nor can it be called clay; for what it was no longer exists, and what does not exist does not adhere at all. So too the soul made flesh is uniform, solidified: the whole is a singularity, an undivided substance. In Christ, however, we find soul and flesh expressed in simple, bare words — that is, soul as soul, flesh as flesh; nowhere soul as flesh or flesh as soul, which is how they would have to be named if they were so blended. Instead, each substance is pronounced separately by Him, distinctly soul and distinctly flesh, precisely to mark the distinction of two natures. "My soul is deeply grieved, even to death" (Matthew 26:38), He says, and: "The bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh" (John 6:51). Now, if soul had been flesh, there would be one fleshy soul or one animate flesh in Christ. But since He distinguishes the kinds — flesh and soul — He shows two. If two, then not one; if not one, then neither soul-flesh nor flesh-soul, for one such blend is a single thing. Unless He also carried a separate soul apart from the one that was flesh, and a separate flesh apart from the one that was soul. But if there is one flesh and one soul — that one sorrowful to death, that one bread for the world's salvation — the count of two substances, distinct in their kind, stands firm, excluding the single hybrid species of soul-flesh.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical distinctions of the Latin text regarding the relationship between soul and flesh. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the conditional and hypothetical structures. Scripture citations (Matthew 26:38 and John 6:51) were correctly identified and added in Pass B to the corresponding Latin clauses.
